content: The recommended dosage of ampicillin-sulbactam for adults is 1.5 g (1 g ampicillin + 0.5 g sulbactam) to 3 g (2 g ampicillin + 1 g sulbactam) every 6 hours, not exceeding a total of 12 g per day. For children and adolescents, the dosage is 100–200 mg of ampicillin per kilogram of body weight per day, administered intravenously and divided into doses every 6 hours. For infants aged 1 month to 1 year, the dosage is 100–150 mg of ampicillin per kilogram per day, given intravenously or intramuscularly in divided doses every 6 hours. For children older than 1 year, the dosage increases to 100–200 mg of ampicillin per kilogram per day, also administered intravenously or intramuscularly in divided doses every 6 hours. In severe cases, such as infections requiring higher doses, children aged 1 month to 1 year may receive 200–300 mg of ampicillin per kilogram per day, while those older than 1 year may receive 200–400 mg per kilogram per day, divided every 6 hours. Adverse effects associated with ampicillin-sulbactam include pain at the intramuscular injection site (16%), diarrhea (3%), pain at the intravenous injection site (3%), thrombophlebitis (3%), and rash (<2%). Other potential side effects include abdominal distension, black hairy tongue, candidiasis, chest pain, chills, dysuria, edema, epistaxis, erythema, fatigue, flatulence, glossitis, headache, itching, malaise, mucosal bleeding, nausea, pseudomembranous colitis, seizures, throat tightness, thrombocytopenia, urinary retention, and vomiting. Gastrointestinal disorders such as abdominal pain, cholestatic hepatitis, cholestasis, hyperbilirubinemia, jaundice, abnormal hepatic function, melena, gastritis, stomatitis, dyspepsia, and Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea have also been reported. Nervous system disorders, including convulsions and dizziness, and respiratory issues such as dyspnea, may occur. Skin reactions include toxic epidermal necrolysis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, angioedema, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP), erythema multiforme, exfoliative dermatitis, urticaria, and linear IgA bullous dermatosis. Serious hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported. Cardiac complications, such as acute myocardial ischemia with or without myocardial infarction, may occur as part of an allergic reaction. Patients with a history of hypersensitivity to the drug or its components, including cephalosporins and carbapenems, should use caution. Dosage adjustments are necessary in cases of renal failure. Prolonged use of the drug may lead to fungal or bacterial superinfections. Hepatic dysfunction, including hepatitis and cholestatic jaundice, has been reported, and while hepatic toxicity is usually reversible, fatalities have occurred. Regular monitoring of hepatic function is recommended, especially in patients with pre-existing hepatic impairment. A generalized dull red maculopapular rash may develop in 5–10% of children 3–14 days after starting therapy. It is important to differentiate this non-allergic ampicillin rash from a hypersensitivity reaction. Patients with infectious mononucleosis are at a higher risk of developing a rash during therapy, and the drug is not recommended for these individuals. Severe skin reactions, such as toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), exfoliative dermatitis, erythema multiforme, and AGEP, may occur. If a skin rash develops, close monitoring is required, and therapy should be discontinued if lesions progress. Ampicillin-sulbactam is classified as pregnancy category B, indicating that controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk. The drug is excreted in breast milk, so caution is advised during lactation. Ampicillin-sulbactam is a combination of a beta-lactamase inhibitor with ampicillin, which interferes with bacterial cell wall synthesis during active replication, resulting in bactericidal activity against susceptible organisms. It serves as an alternative to amoxicillin for patients unable to take oral medications and provides coverage for skin, enteric flora, and anaerobes, though it is not ideal for nosocomial pathogens. Additive effects may occur when combined with aminoglycosides or ciprofloxacin. For intramuscular administration, the solution should be prepared with 2% or 5% lidocaine injection to achieve a concentration of 250 mg ampicillin–125 mg sulbactam/mL and used within 1 hour. For intravenous administration, the solution should be further diluted to 3–45 mg/mL with an appropriate diluent and used within 8 hours. The drug should be administered around the clock to minimize variations in serum levels, with slow intravenous injection over at least 10–15 minutes or infusion over 15–30 minutes. Intramuscular injections should be given deep into a large muscle mass. Intact vials should be stored at temperatures below 30°C. Patients should be monitored closely for adverse effects, and therapy should be adjusted or discontinued as necessary. Regular hepatic function monitoring is essential, particularly in patients with hepatic impairment.
